body: Will do

Starship might not use them internally, but in theory users might specify anything in the starship.toml file.

The regex is taken from https://github.com/chalk/ansi-regex/blob/main/index.js. I included it as-is for the sake of completeness. I don't suppose there'll be noticeable penalty for searching all the characters?

I mean yes, two starship invocations will definitely be more time-consuming than one. 

I think we can still go with this for now, and when #3467 finally lands, we could go with the approach in #4208 as a performance improvement.

> Do you know if there is a notable difference between this and the ANSI escape I used?

Is there any documentation on `1B7` and `1B8`? I couldn't figure out how to use it in PowerShell.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Fp_Escape_sequences It does seem to be former private use, so it might be worse.
I'll try testing that, too. It might also be worth to compile this regex.
Is there an easy method to spawn both executables concurrently?
I guess for clarity and familiarity, the `[s` and `[u` would be better, since all the Google search results for cursor control show these sequences.

There are ways using Jobs and Threads, but they're ugly (see https://stackoverflow.com/questions/4016451/can-powershell-run-commands-in-parallel) and I'm not sure the overhead of these would justify their usage here.

body: Done

> Please also avoid printing the rprompt if it wouldn't fit like my PR did.

Done

I probably should have tested this earlier, but I just noticed that if the last prompt line contains an emoji or any double-width (or any non-single-width character), this calculation will break.
Does PowerShell have any Unicode-aware string width functions via .NET that we could use instead?

Apart from that, the changes in this PR look good to me.

I tried some emojis and double-width characters (◌️, 😂, 😢) and they seem to be working well.

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/46838874/211205388-fb880948-656d-4b47-81e5-3d7d59389354.png)

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/46838874/211205510-936c4671-42c0-46c5-8c04-b0d9ef62f78c.png)

Do you have any characters I can test?
`❌` from the status triggered a rendering issue in iTerm for me: You can try this: ``` [character] success_symbol = "❌❌❌❌❌❌❌❌❌❌❌" ```

Hmm, I can repro the issue using this symbol. I have tried searching online, but I can't find a proper method to find out the number of terminal boxes a character occupies, in C#. There are ways to find out code point or grapheme lengths, but they all mean different things 😢
Starship itself uses the maximum code point width per grapheme to approximate character widths, so using something along those line should be fine.
Could you point me where the code for that lives? I can try translating it to PowerShell.

It's defined in `print.rs`:
https://github.com/starship/starship/blob/master/src/print.rs#L21-L48

Okay, I'll admit I have no idea what's happening there 😅. It seems to be using a third-party library and its members.

Could we handle this in a new issue/PR?

> Could we handle this in a new issue/PR?

I would rather not, we're already getting quite a few issues because `$fill` doesn't always calculate widths as expected.
At least this should use some kind of string width function like `wcswidth` verbatim.

Unfortunately Windows or .NET doesn't have a `wcswidth` equivalent. Most portable implementations of `wcswidth` I found online use lookup tables of code points. Even the unicode-width Rust library (used in `print.rs`) has a table. Implementing that in the PowerShell init script does not sound very feasible to me.

In that case, I would rather go with #4208. I'll try to push the `--profile` PR forward and rendering custom target pairs after that to allow for transient rprompts in pwsh. Hopefully this can work out without a breaking change to transient prompt configuration.
